Let’s dive into Chapter 8: Overcoming Resistance and Sustaining Change.
Even when everyone’s got good intentions, trying to shift the way people make decisions almost always bumps up against some resistance. Maybe folks worry about losing their autonomy, or maybe they just like the comfort of doing things the way they've always done them. Change, especially when it comes to habits, isn’t easy—and it takes both patience and a few smart strategies to really make it stick.
First up? Empathy. Change isn’t just about logic and new procedures—it’s a real emotional journey. If you’re leading the charge, it helps to listen closely, acknowledge people’s concerns, and invite them to help shape what the new way of working looks like. When people feel heard and respected, they’re a lot more likely to get on board instead of digging in their heels.
Another important piece is making the benefits of evidence-based decision-making crystal clear. Don’t just talk about it—show it. Celebrate those early wins, like when a new checklist or a premortem saves a project from a big mistake. Sharing real success stories helps everyone see that this isn’t just theory—it actually works in practice.
So, how can organizations lower the barriers even more? Well, start small. Try out new tools or processes with one team or department before rolling them out everywhere. Offer training and coaching so people feel confident, not lost. And don’t forget to align incentives—make sure thoughtful, evidence-based decisions actually get recognized and rewarded.
Here’s something important to remember: the fear of failure can be a huge roadblock. In lots of places, mistakes get stigmatized, so people hide problems or avoid taking risks. But what if you flipped the script and treated failure as a learning opportunity? Leaders who do this—by encouraging open conversations about what went wrong—help create a culture where honest reflection and experimentation are not just allowed, but valued.
Picture a software company hosting regular “failure forums,” where teams openly discuss what didn’t work and what they’ve learned. Over time, this kind of openness helps everyone lower their guard and focus on getting better together.
Sustaining change isn’t a one-time thing—it’s an ongoing process. It takes vigilance, positive reinforcement, and a willingness to adapt as new challenges pop up. But with persistence and a caring mindset, organizations can build decision-making habits that actually last.
